title: Pond Dipping
strapline: Dip the net, tip it gently into the tray — and hold your breath to see what wriggles out.
intent: A pond is a hidden world teeming with life children would never otherwise meet, and dipping it lets them discover, up close, that water is full of creatures.
The care it takes — a gentle net, a quick look, a safe return — grows deep respect for tiny, fragile living things.
Watching and identifying pond creatures builds real knowledge of habitats, life cycles and how living things depend on water.
Studying, counting and comparing the catch is close observation and early classifying — legs and no legs, fast and still, big and small.
The whole experience is charged with patience, wonder and the thrill of not knowing what the net will bring up.
Naming and describing the creatures brings rich vocabulary — pondweed, tadpole, larva, gills, wriggle, dart, habitat.
implementation: Set up safely at a shallow pond or a large water tray seeded with pond life — nets, white trays, magnifiers, and clear rules about gentle hands and safe edges.
Dip, tip the catch into a tray of pond water, and simply look before naming anything: 'What can you see moving? How many legs has it got?'
Model care and calm: 'It's very tiny and it lives in the water, so we look quickly and put it straight back home.'
Support close study — magnifiers, an identification chart, wondering together what each creature might be and what it does.
Bring in maths and sorting — count the creatures in the tray, group the ones that swim and the ones that crawl, compare which is biggest.
Return every creature to the water together, and follow the life-cycle story over weeks — the frogspawn, the tadpoles, the tiny froglets.
key_questions: What can you see moving? How many legs has it got?
Which creatures swim, and which ones crawl?
Which is the biggest thing in the tray?
How should we hold it so we keep it safe?
Where do you think this creature lives, and what does it do?

impact.text: Children discover that water is full of creatures and build knowledge of habitats and life cycles.
Children handle fragile living things with a gentle net, a quick look and a safe return.
Children study, count and compare the catch — close observation and early classifying.
Children wait patiently with wonder and the thrill of not knowing what the net will bring.
Children gain rich vocabulary — pondweed, tadpole, larva, gills, wriggle, dart, habitat.

enhancements: Nets, white trays and magnifiers, with clear rules about gentle hands and safe edges.
An identification chart for wondering what each creature might be.
A count-and-sort of the tray — swimmers and crawlers, biggest and smallest.
A life-cycle watch over weeks — frogspawn, tadpoles, tiny froglets.
A large seeded water tray indoors if a real pond isn't reachable.

active_learning: Children wait, dip again and study patiently, staying absorbed in the slow work of finding and watching.
